questions.question: Distinguish between economic growth and development, and between standard of living and quality of life, using South African examples to show why the distinctions matter.
questions.expected_answer: Economic growth means the economy produces a larger total of goods and services than before; development means people's quality of life actually improves — health, education, safety, services and dignity as well as income. Growth is necessary for development but not sufficient, because new wealth can pool in few hands: a factory can double its output while the surrounding community sees no new clinics, schools or jobs, which is growth without development. Standard of living is the material side — what income buys, such as housing, appliances and services — while quality of life is the whole picture, adding health, education, safety, environment and freedom. A well-paid miner working in a dangerous, dusty shaft has a reasonable standard of living but a poor quality of life. The distinctions matter because South Africa's totals and averages look middle-income while the lived reality for millions is deprivation, so any honest judgement must look past money alone.

questions.question: Explain how GDP, GDP per capita, the Gini coefficient and the HDI each measure development, and show what each one reveals about South Africa that the others miss.
questions.expected_answer: GDP is the total value of goods and services produced within a country's borders in a year; GNP counts production by the country's citizens and companies wherever they operate, so the Toyota plant in Durban is in South Africa's GDP but Japan's GNP. Dividing GDP by population gives GDP per capita — output per person — which removes the distortion of population size and places South Africa around 6 000 US dollars, a middle-income figure. But per capita is an average and hides distribution, so the Gini coefficient measures inequality from 0 (perfect equality) to 1 (one person earns everything); South Africa's roughly 0,63 is among the world's highest and reveals the deep poverty the average conceals. The HDI combines life expectancy, years of schooling and income per person into a score between 0 and 1; South Africa's roughly 0,71 shows relatively strong income and schooling dragged down by health, exposing the gap between wealth and wellbeing that the money measures cannot see. Together the four numbers answer three questions: how much is produced, how it is shared, and what lives are actually like.

questions.question: Evaluate the usefulness of the Brandt line today, and use the idea of a development continuum to classify South Africa's development status with supporting evidence.
questions.expected_answer: The Brandt line of 1980 divided the world into a rich North and a poor South, dipping to include Australia and New Zealand. It remains a useful first sketch of global inequality, but it froze a snapshot that has blurred: South Korea and Singapore, south of the line, now outrank many European economies, so the two-box world no longer holds. The truthful picture is a continuum, with countries occupying every position from lowest to highest development, and with sharp differences inside single countries — Sandton and Diepsloot share one metro, and Gauteng's economy dwarfs the former homeland districts of the Eastern Cape. On this continuum South Africa is best classified as a developing country, specifically a newly industrialised, upper-middle-income country: evidence for relative development includes an industrialised economy, the JSE, GDP per capita around 6 000 US dollars and an HDI of about 0,71; evidence of underdevelopment includes unemployment above 30 per cent, a Gini coefficient near 0,63 and life expectancy in the mid-sixties. The balanced conclusion — a developing NIC containing pockets of MEDC prosperity and pockets of LEDC deprivation — earns the evaluation marks because it is argued from indicators rather than impressions.
